verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, a maskil, of the sons of Korah.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster's hand: a song to make wise, from the sons of Korah.
verses.directors_commentary: This line is not part of the poem's voice: it is the label on the scroll, and the Hebrew numbering counts it as verse 1, where the KJV leaves it unnumbered as 42:0. Everything after it is shifted by one against the KJV. Three words are worth knowing. 'Choirmaster' (לַמְנַצֵּחַ) is a title for the one who directs the Temple singers; the KJV's 'chief Musician' is a fair rendering. 'Maskil' is left untranslated in the KJV and ASV because nobody is sure what it means: the root is 'to be insightful', so it is either 'a poem that instructs' (Metzudat David, Meiri) or a plain genre name, like 'ballad' (Ibn Ezra mentions both). 'Of the sons of Korah' (לִבְנֵי קֹרַח) is a guild of Levite singers who traced their descent from the rebel Korah, whose own house was swallowed by the earth while his sons did not die (Num 26:11, cited by Rashi). The preposition ל is ambiguous: 'by', 'for', or 'belonging to'. Tell the actors that the speaker of this psalm sings in the voice of someone far from the sanctuary, the very sanctuary where this guild stood to sing.

philological_notes.note: A psalm-label of uncertain sense, from the root 'to be wise, to have insight'. Read either as a causative ('one that makes wise', so a teaching-poem) or as a plain genre name.
A guild of Levite singers named for Korah's line, which survived his rebellion. The ל can mean 'by' or 'for'.

verses.translation_literal: Like a deer [which] pants over channels of water, so my soul pants to you, O God.
verses.translation_dramatic: As a deer cries out for the running streams, panting for the water that rushes there, so my soul cries out to you, O God.
verses.directors_commentary: The image opens on an animal in need: a deer at the water's edge, breathing hard, the verb itself an animal sound. The Hebrew verb עָרַג is a noise-word, used for the call of an animal, like 'lowing' for cattle (Rashi, Metzudat Zion compare roaring and bellowing), not the polite 'panteth' of the KJV. Ibn Ezra and Radak add the background: the deer eats snakes, its belly burns, and it seeks water to cool itself; Radak adds that deer live in the desert, where water is scarce. 'Channels of water' (אֲפִיקֵי מַיִם) are, in Metzudat Zion's words, the places where water runs with force; Ibn Ezra says the deer seeks 'strong waters', and Radak 'waters that run there'. The thirst is therefore not for a still pool but for living, moving water, which prepares the 'living God' of the next verse. Grammar adds a detail the English hides: 'deer' (אַיָּל) is masculine, but the verb 'pants' (תַּעֲרֹג) is feminine, and Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri discuss whether the verse means the species, male and female alike (Rashi sees both). The same verb is then used of the speaker's 'soul' (נֶפֶשׁ), which in Hebrew means throat and breath before it means anything spiritual: the speaker longs with the whole body. The KJV's 'after thee' softens the direction; the Hebrew says 'to you' (אֵלֶיךָ), toward a person.

philological_notes.note: An animal's cry of longing, used for the deer's call at the water. The same word is used twice, once for the deer and once for the soul, so the comparison is made through the sound itself.
Channels where water runs with force: flowing, moving water, not a standing pool.
Soul, throat, breath: the part of a person that takes in water and air. Thirst for God is meant bodily.

verses.translation_literal: My soul thirsts for God, for the living God: when shall I come and see the face of God?
verses.translation_dramatic: My whole being is parched for God, for the living God. When? When may I come, and see his face?
verses.directors_commentary: 'Thirsts' is the choice the poem has made: Radak notes that the verse does not say 'hungers', because a person can go days without food but not without water, so thirst is the need that cannot wait. 'Living God' (אֵל חַי) is a pointed phrase: Radak says it is said because the other gods are dead, and Meiri adds that the nations also call their idols 'gods'. The speaker's God moves, answers, is alive. The last clause is the verse's turn, and the KJV blurs it. Hebrew וְאֵרָאֶה פְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים is literally 'and I shall see the face of God', the standard idiom for coming into the sanctuary (the traditional vowel pointing makes the verb a passive-reflexive, 'be seen, appear', but the idiom means the same). 'Appear before God' in the KJV and ASV smooths it to a courtroom appearance; the Targum goes further and says 'see the glory of the Shekhinah'. Rashi and Radak read it as the pilgrimage to the Temple three times a year, to the 'face' of God, meaning the presence in the sanctuary. The opposite of that is exile, which is where the speaker is.

philological_notes.note: 'The living God', set against idols that do not move or answer.

Literally 'and I shall see the face of God', a pilgrimage idiom for entering the sanctuary. The form is pointed as a passive-reflexive ('be seen', 'appear'), which is why the KJV has 'appear before God'; the sense of the idiom is the same.

verses.translation_literal: My tear has been to me bread by day and by night, when they say to me all the day, Where [is] your God?
verses.translation_dramatic: Tears have become my bread, morning and night, while all day long they ask me: Where is your God?
verses.directors_commentary: 'Bread' (לֶחֶם) is the Hebrew word for food in general and for the daily loaf in particular: the poor ate it twice, morning and evening, and tears have replaced both meals. The KJV's 'meat' is archaic for food and is now misleading, since modern readers hear 'meat'. Rashi and Metzudat David read the image as grief that fills the stomach so the speaker cannot eat, like Hannah in 1 Sam 1:7; Ibn Ezra offers the other reading, that the speaker cries at his meal. Notice the singular, 'my tear' (דִמְעָתִי), where the KJV says 'tears': the Hebrew makes a single tear stand for all of them. The taunt, 'Where is your God?', is the center of the psalm and returns in v. 11. It is a taunt only in a world where a god is expected to be located and to act: a people whose god has an image in a temple can point to it, and the speaker's God has no image to point to and, in exile, no temple (Radak: they say, if he were the true God, he would have saved you). 'When they say' is a temporal clause with the verb in the infinitive (בֶּאֱמֹר); the 'all the day' continues without interruption, so the actors should deliver it as a drumbeat.

philological_notes.note: Bread, the staple food, so 'food' in general. The KJV's 'meat' once meant this, but now means flesh.
The mockery of the enemies: 'Where is your God?'. Repeated in verse 11. In the taunt the divine title is the generic 'elohim', as the nations would speak.

verses.translation_literal: These [things] I remember, and I pour out my soul upon me: how I passed along in the throng, I walked slowly with them to the house of God, with the sound of a ringing shout and thanksgiving, a multitude keeping festival.
verses.translation_dramatic: This is what I remember, and my soul pours out of me like water: how I used to move along inside the crowd, walking slowly with them to the house of God, to the sound of singing and thanksgiving, a great multitude keeping the feast.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the memory that undoes him: the pilgrim road. 'These things' are the pilgrimage festivals, three times a year, when the whole land walked up to the sanctuary (Radak, Ibn Ezra). 'Pour out my soul' (אֶשְׁפְּכָה נַפְשִׁי) is a liquid image: the soul spills like water, which answers the dryness of verse 2, and Meiri explains it as the soul dissolving into water and leaving through the eyes as tears. This verse is textually one of the hardest in the psalm, and the English versions split. 'I passed along in the throng' (אֶעֱבֹר בַּסָּךְ) uses a rare word, סָךְ, which Rashi derives from 'count' (a counted crowd) or from 'covering' (a covered wagon, like a booth, for the notable travelers), Ibn Ezra from the Temple's 'covered way' on the Sabbath. The KJV 'I had gone with the multitude' has smoothed all of this into a single clear scene; the YLT 'into the booth' keeps the other possibility. The next word, אֶדַּדֵּם, is a rare form:'I walked slowly with them' (Rashi compares the mother who leads her child by the hand, 'leading calves and foals'; Metzudat Zion says 'slowly and gently'); the ASV chose 'led them'. A pilgrim crowd moves at the pace of the slowest, and the speaker lingers with the procession, not ahead of it. 'Ringing shout' (רִנָּה) is a loud cry; 'thanksgiving' (תּוֹדָה) is what is offered at the altar. 'Keeping festival' (חוֹגֵג) is the verb behind the Arabic hajj, and it means to make a pilgrimage and to celebrate in dance, not merely to 'keep holyday' as the KJV has it.

philological_notes.note: A rare word: 'in the throng' (from a sense of 'sum, number'), or 'in the covering' (booth, or covered cart). Disputed.

'I walked slowly with them', from דדה, a verb of slow, gentle walking (used of a mother leading a child). Rashi also records readings from 'friend' and from 'be silent'; the traditional pointing and the pilgrim context favor the walking sense.
To keep a pilgrimage festival, and by extension to dance and celebrate; the root of 'chag', festival.

verses.translation_literal: Why are you bowed down, my soul, and [why] do you roar over me? Wait for God, for yet I shall give thanks to him, [for] the salvations of his face.
verses.translation_dramatic: Why are you bent so low, my soul? Why do you rage and murmur inside me? Wait for God. I will thank him yet, for the rescue that comes with his face.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker turns and addresses his own soul, which is the dramatic hinge of the psalm: the voice that cried out in the first verses is now talked to like a child who is overwrought. 'Bowed down' (תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי) means to sink and stoop; Rashi and Metzudat Zion link it to the verb of bowing to the dust. 'Are in turmoil' (תֶּהֱמִי) is a sound-word, the cry of a restless sea, a cooing dove, a crowd, so the soul is not only low but noisy: a mix of collapse and roar. 'Wait' (הוֹחִילִי) is the verb of hope, a patient waiting (Rashi: wait and look for the redemption; Metzudat Zion ties it to 'hope'). The ending is a famous difficulty. The Hebrew says 'the salvations of his face' (יְשׁוּעוֹת פָּנָיו), and the KJV smooths it to 'the help of his countenance'. The YLT's 'The salvation of my countenance -- My God!' here is the wording of the refrain in v. 12 (פָּנַי וֵאלֹהָי), not of the Hebrew of this verse, which has 'his face'. The 'face' of God is again the presence of v. 3: salvation is the effect of being in his presence. Ibn Ezra and Meiri take it as 'by his saving acts', and note that 'his face' stands for him in person, so that the rescue comes from him alone. The plural 'salvations' stresses repeated rescues. An actor should hear the argument in the verse: pity, then rebuke, then promise.

philological_notes.note: To bow down, be bent low. The form is a reflexive (hitpolel): 'you bow yourself'.
Wait in hope, expect with confidence. Related to 'tochelet', hope.
'The salvations of his face': rescue that comes with his presence. A famously difficult phrase; the refrain in v. 12 reads 'the salvation of my face and my God'.

verses.translation_literal: My God, upon me my soul is bowed down; therefore I remember you from the land of the Jordan and the Hermons, from Mount Mizar.
verses.translation_dramatic: My God, my soul is bent low inside me, and so I remember you from here: from the land of the Jordan, from the peaks of Hermon, from the little mountain, Mizar.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the geography shows where the speaker stands. He is not in the Temple: he remembers God 'from the land of the Jordan', the far north and east, the headwaters country below Hermon, at the farthest edge of Israel from Jerusalem, or even beyond it. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as the land from which pilgrims walked up, 'beyond the Jordan eastward'; Rashi and Meiri see the names as places of God's past deeds (the Jordan dried at Joshua 3:16, Sinai the 'little' mountain). The KJV gives 'the Hermonites' for חֶרְמוֹנִים, which is a mistake produced by guessing at a rare plural: the word is a plural of the mountain, 'the Hermons', the several summits of the massif, and Ibn Ezra says so ('mountains'). Mizar means 'small' or 'little', a pun on the huge Hermon beside it; Rashi's tradition makes Sinai 'the little one among the mountains', and the Targum says so; Radak admits the peak 'is not found'. The Hebrew text has the tone of homesickness in a cold place: snow-fed water, high rock. Tell the actors this verse is a map for a man standing in the wrong place, remembering the right one.

philological_notes.note: The plural of Hermon, 'the Hermons': the several peaks of the Hermon range. The KJV 'Hermonites' treats it as a people.
'The little mountain'; a peak otherwise unknown. The name means 'small', which sits against the great Hermon beside it.

verses.translation_literal: Deep to deep calls, at the voice of your channels; all your breakers and your waves over me have passed.
verses.translation_dramatic: Deep calls to deep, at the thunder of your waterfalls; every breaker of yours, every wave, has gone over my head.
verses.directors_commentary: The scene changes from thirst to flood, and the speaker is now the one under water. 'Deep' (תְּהוֹם) is the primeval ocean of Genesis 1:2, the chaos water under the world, so 'deep calls to deep' is chaos answering chaos: one trouble calls the next (Rashi, Metzudat David). The word 'waterspouts' in the KJV is a nautical guess; צִנּוֹר is a pipe, a gutter or a water-channel, and Rashi's old French gloss and Metzudat Zion both say a channel through which water pours, so 'at the sound of your channels' is a roaring torrent coming off the Hermon heights Ibn Ezra describes. 'Your channels', 'your breakers', 'your waves': three times the Hebrew says 'yours', and it is God's water that overwhelms the speaker; Radak notes that God sent them. 'All' and the perfect 'have passed over me' mark finality: the speaker is not standing in the flood, but past the point of rescue, drowned. 'Breakers' (מִשְׁבָּרִים) are the waves that break (Rashi, Metzudat Zion); 'waves' (גַּלִּים) the rolling swell; the KJV 'billows' is an old word for the same. This is the sound-world the director should build: the roar is both outer and inner, and the voice must be heard to go under.

philological_notes.note: 'Deep to deep': the primeval waters calling to one another. Read as one trouble summoning the next.
A pipe or channel through which water rushes, a 'waterfall' or cataract; the KJV 'waterspouts' is a guess. Radak also reads it as the clouds that pour rain.
'Breakers': waves that rise and break. Same root as 'break'.

verses.translation_literal: By day YHWH commands his loyal love, and by night his song [is] with me, a prayer to the God of my life.
verses.translation_dramatic: By day the LORD sends out his faithful love; by night his song is with me, a prayer to the God who is my life.
verses.directors_commentary: A pivot of trust inside the lament. 'Commands' (יְצַוֶּה) is the verb of the commander: God gives an order and his steadfast love goes out to carry it, like a servant. The KJV's 'lovingkindness' is a Coverdale coinage for חֶסֶד, which is covenant loyalty, the faithfulness one party owes the other in a treaty; 'will command' in the KJV also misses that the verb is a plain imperfect that can describe a habit as well as a promise. Note that this is the first place in the psalm where the divine name YHWH appears; until now the poem has said only 'God' (Elohim), the word the enemies also use. The speaker's name for God, the covenant name, is what comes with loyalty. 'By day' and 'by night' echo verse 4, where tears were his bread 'by day and by night': the same two times now carry a different gift. The written text here has שִׁירָה, read as 'his song' (שִׁירוֹ); Rashi, drawing on the Masorah, treats the written form as 'his encampment' and so 'his camp is with us' (he notes the midrash that takes it as 'song'). 'The God of my life' is the God who gives it and keeps it.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, faithful love: more than the KJV's 'lovingkindness'. Here God 'commands' it, sends it out like a messenger.

Qere 'his song'; the written text (Ketiv) has a final ה, שִׁירָה. Rashi, citing the Masorah, reads the written form as 'lodging, encampment' (as in the Targum's 'and he encamped' at Exod 19:2), and records the midrash that reads 'song'.

verses.translation_literal: I will say to God, my rock: Why have you forgotten me? Why [do] I go about darkened, under the oppression of an enemy?
verses.translation_dramatic: I will say to God, my rock: Why have you forgotten me? Why must I walk in black, pressed down by an enemy?
verses.directors_commentary: Here the speaker says outright what the trust of verse 9 had held back: 'Why have you forgotten me?'. The same mouth that praised God's command of love now accuses him of forgetting; the psalm does not smooth over the contradiction, and the actors should not either. 'My rock' (סַלְעִי) is not a mere metaphor of strength. A סֶלַע is the cliff in the wilderness where a fugitive hides, the one place a hunted man cannot be reached, and Radak and Meiri read it as the God who used to be his stronghold, so the accusation is the sharper: the rock has gone away. 'Mourning' (קֹדֵר) is literally 'dark, blackened': a mourner in sackcloth or dark clothes, with the face darkened (Rashi compares the prophets' 'it will be dark over them', Mic 3:6; Ibn Ezra, 'like a mourner who wears darkness'). The KJV's 'mourning' is right in sense, though it loses the darkness. 'Oppression of the enemy' (לַחַץ אוֹיֵב) is a squeezing, a crowding press; the KJV has the definite article ('the enemy') where the Hebrew is indefinite, a single hostile power. Radak notes the two 'why' words are pointed differently, the first light and stressed at the end, the second doubled; the pause between them is the gasp the actor should play.

philological_notes.note: 'My rock': the crag, a hiding place for a fugitive. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'my strength'.
'Dark, blackened': the look of a mourner in dark garments. Related to 'Kedar', the 'dark' tents.
Squeezing, pressure; oppression. Metzudat Zion says 'distress'.

verses.translation_literal: With a crushing in my bones my adversaries have taunted me, when they say to me all the day, Where [is] your God?
verses.translation_dramatic: It is like a killing blow in my bones, the way my enemies jeer at me, all day long: Where is your God?
verses.directors_commentary: The taunt of verse 4 returns, with the pain placed inside the body. The key word is בְּרֶצַח, and the KJV's 'as with a sword' is an interpretation, not a translation: רֶצַח is 'murder', the act of killing, and the Hebrew says 'in a murder in my bones', so the insult feels like a killing. Radak reads it as a noun for the weapon, 'a killing-sword'; Rashi, Metzudat David and Meiri say it is 'as if they were killing me', as the sword would. The BBE's 'crushing' matches the other meaning ('shattering'), which fits the STEPBible gloss. Either way the target is the bones, the frame of the body and the seat of the self (Radak: they are the foundations of the body); in Jeremiah 20:9 the word is a fire shut up in the bones. The adversaries (צוֹרְרַי) are those who press the speaker into a narrow place, from the same root as 'tight, distress'. 'Taunted' (חֵרְפוּנִי) is not mere reproach; it is public shaming, and it is aimed at the speaker's relationship with God, the one thing that he cannot show them. Contrast with verse 4: there the taunt made him weep; here it breaks him.

philological_notes.note: 'In a killing': rendered by the traditional commentators as 'as with a sword that kills', or 'as if murder'. The KJV 'as with a sword' interprets it.
To taunt, reproach publicly; a shaming speech.

verses.translation_literal: Why are you bowed down, my soul, and why do you roar over me? Wait for God, for yet I shall give thanks to him, the salvation of my face and my God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Why are you bent so low, my soul? Why do you rage inside me? Wait for God. I will thank him yet, my rescue, the lifting of my face, and my God.
verses.directors_commentary: The refrain returns with two small changes, and the changes are the point. In verse 6 the question has one 'why' and ends with God's face ('the salvations of his face'). Here the second question gains its own 'and why' (וּמַה), so the rebuke is a little firmer, and the final clause moves from third person to first: 'the salvation of my face, and my God' (יְשׁוּעֹת פָּנַי וֵאלֹהָי). The KJV 'health of my countenance' is an old sense of 'health' as salvation. What the Hebrew says is that God is the salvation of 'my face': the face that was cast down in grief, darkened in verse 10, is the face he will lift. Ibn Ezra, Rashi and Radak all read it so: 'my face and my God' means the one who is my light and my help. The last word, 'and my God', is possessive and personal, in reply to the enemies' 'your God' in verse 11: where they say 'your God' at a distance, the speaker ends by saying 'my God'. The actors should play it as an answer. Note also that the line after it, the refrain a third time, is in the next psalm, so this is not a conclusion yet.

philological_notes.note: 'The salvation of my face': God as the one who lifts the downcast face. The form is plural construct ('salvations'), with the sense of repeated acts. Compare v. 6, 'salvations of his face'.
'And my God': the speaker closes with the possessive, in answer to the enemies' 'your God'.
